When I was a young girl, I lost my mother. There was nobody to look after and guide me. My father was a busy man and got married again. In those days people never considered education essential for girls, so I never went to school. I got married very young and had children. I became very busy. Later I had grandchildren and always felt so much happiness in cooking and feeding all of you. questions.subject: English
questions.stem: An old woman in your colony has never been to school and has just learnt to read at the age of sixty-two. Write an article of about 100 words for your school magazine on why age is no bar to learning, using her example.

markingPoints.description: Content: the article gives a clear view that age is no bar to learning and supports it with the example of a woman who learnt to read at sixty-two
Format: the correct format of a magazine article, that is, a striking heading and short paragraphs
Organisation: a clear beginning that states the main point, a middle part that gives the example and a short concluding thought
Accuracy: correct spelling, punctuation and capital letters, and a formal and simple tone
Expression: simple sentences and suitable vocabulary that hold the reader's attention

answerScheme.modelAnswer:
Learning Is Never Too Late

When my grandmother was sixty-two years old, she decided to learn the Kannada alphabet. She had never been to school, and for years she had felt helpless because she could not read. Her own granddaughter became her teacher, and every day she read, repeated, wrote and recited. On Saraswati Puja day during Dassara she opened a gift and read the title Kashi Yatre by Triveni by herself. She then touched her granddaughter's feet and said she was touching the feet of a teacher. Age is only a number. What matters is the determination to begin.

evidence: at this age of sixty-two you want to learn the alphabet?
For learning there is no age bar.
She would read, repeat, write, and recite.

VILLAGE NOTICE BOARD
ADULT EVENING CLASS

All residents are informed that an evening class for adults who have never been to school will begin in the village hall. The class will meet every evening after the day's work is over, and there is no age bar for learning. Adults who wish to join may enrol at the village office at any time during the week. Sd/- Programme Officer

She adds that such ideas are always open to improvement and often change as new evidence becomes available, and that this openness is what makes science reliable.

Name, in order, the levels the chart shows, beginning with cells of a similar kind and ending with organ systems. questions.topic: Testing Thomson’s model: The gold foil experiment
questions.stem:
Rutherford's atomic model has the electrons revolving around a nucleus, rather like planets orbiting the Sun, so it is called the planetary model. Rutherford found that the nucleus is extremely small, about one lakh times smaller than the atom. His model explained the results of the gold foil experiment better than Thomson's, but it left one big question unanswered: why are atoms stable? A particle moving in a circular path is accelerating, and an accelerating electron should lose energy, spiral inward and fall into the nucleus. If that happened, atoms would collapse and would not exist, yet in reality atoms are stable.

Answer these questions:
1. Why is Rutherford's model of the atom called the planetary model?
2. A student argues that atoms are stable, so the accelerating electron must be losing energy and falling into the nucleus. Why does the model fail to explain this?

answerScheme.modelAnswer: (1) Because the electrons revolve around the nucleus like planets orbiting the Sun. (2) The model cannot explain stability: if the accelerating electron lost energy it would spiral inward and fall into the nucleus, so atoms would collapse, yet in reality atoms are stable and matter around us stays intact.

Answer these questions on the case:

Farhan's grandmother keeps bread and roti in a plastic box on the shelf. One warm day she left the box untouched and, after three days, fuzzy patches had spread over the food. Farhan carried a little of the mould on a needle to a microscope slide and added cotton blue stain so that he could see it better. His teacher then told him that fungi grow very fast by spore formation, degrade organic wastes and pollutants, and that many antibiotics, including penicillin and amoxicillin, are derived from fungi.

(a) What did Farhan add to the mould on the slide, and what was that addition meant to do? (b) State how fungi manage to grow so quickly, and name two antibiotics that are derived from them. (c) Farhan's family wants to throw away the bread on which these fungi grew. Using his teacher's account, explain why fungi are useful to society, giving two reasons.

answerScheme.modelAnswer: (a) He added cotton blue stain, a coloured dye that helps him see the mould better. (b) Fungi grow very fast by spore formation; penicillin and amoxicillin. (c) They degrade organic wastes and pollutants and remove heavy metals from industrial wastes, and the antibiotics derived from them save countless lives from bacterial infections.

questions.subject: Science
questions.stem:
Over the monsoon break, Riya's family left cooked food out in the kitchen for a day in warm weather, and it began to smell and grow fuzzy patches. Her uncle said the food had made these microbes on its own, because for long people thought living things arose spontaneously from non-living matter. Her aunt disagreed. She reminded the family that experiments by Louis Pasteur proved that new life always comes from pre-existing life. Pasteur found the germ theory of disease and strengthened the cell theory, that all cells arise from pre-existing cells, and his work led to practices like food and instrument sterilisation.

(a) State what Pasteur's experiments proved about where new life comes from. (b) Name the germ theory he found and the theory he strengthened, stating what each one says. (c) Riya's uncle is certain that the stale food produced these microbes by itself. Using what Pasteur proved, explain why he is wrong, and state the two practices his work led to.

answerScheme.modelAnswer: (a) That new life always comes from pre-existing life. (b) The germ theory of disease, and the cell theory, that all cells arise from pre-existing cells. (c) The food is non-living, so it cannot give rise to life on its own; the microbes came from pre-existing life, so food and instruments should be sterilised.

questions.stem:
Wheat has been grown on Nandita's family farm for generations, and her grandfather chose each year's seed stock from the plants with the most desirable characters. When a disease began to damage the crop, Nandita's father removed the stamens from flowers of the crop plant, tied a bagging around them so that the plant's own pollen could not reach them, and carried pollen by hand from a plant that already resisted the disease. This year the farm also grew a new variety whose DNA carries the genetic material of a desired character placed there by scientists, and the plants that grew from it were high yielding and resisted the disease.

(a) Name the plant breeding method Nandita's father used and state why he removed the stamens and tied a bagging around the flowers. (b) Nandita's grandfather chose the seed stock, her father transferred pollen and scientists altered the DNA. Explain how these three approaches each bring a desired character into the crop grown on the farm.

answerScheme.modelAnswer: (a) Artificial hybridisation; removing the stamens and bagging the flower prevents self-pollination, so only the transferred pollen fertilises it. (b) Selective breeding works by choosing which plants reproduce, artificial hybridisation by hand-transferring pollen from a chosen plant, and genetic engineering by inserting the desired character into the DNA, so each changes what the next crop inherits.

While on a visit to a wildlife sanctuary, Tanya learns that the Lion-tailed macaque and the Neelakurinji plant occur only in India and nowhere else naturally. A forestry officer then tells her that four such regions have been identified in the country: the Western Ghats, Indo-Burma, the Himalayas and Sundaland. (a) What is the name for species that occur only in one region of the world and are found nowhere else naturally? (c) These areas are rich in number and in the diversity of organisms; they support food webs and help ecosystems remain healthy.

She also mentions that some features cannot be seen at all and have to be studied through DNA. Ishan wonders whether two organisms that look completely different could still be related.

Rohan’s family runs a shop in India. The shop’s rooftop solar panels work well all year, because India lies in the tropical and sub-tropical regions and so receives abundant sunlight throughout the year. Scientists take this into account when they study the solar constant, the quantity that helps them understand the Earth’s energy balance and climate. 2. State the two everyday things that this amount of energy is equal to.

answerScheme.modelAnswer: (1) Dark surfaces absorb more sunlight, while light coloured surfaces reflect more and stay comparatively cooler. (2) Albedo; the word comes from Latin and means whiteness. On the other side of the year, a school inland in India keeps its own diary of the wind. From October onwards the mornings are cool, and the wind that used to arrive from the sea stops coming. A Class 9 teacher is worried about two words that students keep swapping. The first is used for people who share a common territory, a culture and a shared sense of belonging, and who settle their differences and pass on their ways of doing things. (b) Society is primarily regulated by customs and practices rather than formal laws, whereas a State is based on rules and laws. (c) Such political systems developed gradually as societies became larger and more complex.

questions.stem:
An exhibition has been planned on the earliest Indian past, but the curator cannot put a single date on the wall for the oldest hymns. Scholars keep arguing about when they were composed, and the estimates run from the fifth millennium BCE to the second millennium BCE. The museum knows only that these hymns were recited out loud for several centuries before anyone wrote them down. Even more puzzling, the script of the Harappans of the Sindhu–Sarasvatī civilisation has still not been deciphered, so what those people left behind cannot be read. A visitor asks whether the exhibition should be dropped altogether.

(a) State the range of estimates that historians give for the date of composition of the Ṛigveda. (b) Explain why the Vedas are called the earliest known corpus of Indian literature, and state how Vedic literature came to be written down. (c) The curator still wants the exhibition; explain what can be worked out about the Ṛigveda and the Sindhu–Sarasvatī civilisation despite the undeciphered script.

answerScheme.modelAnswer: (a) Estimates range from the fifth millennium BCE to the second millennium BCE. (b) The Vedas are the earliest known corpus because the Harappan script is still undeciphered; Vedic literature existed in oral form for several centuries before it was written down. (c) The Ṛigveda was composed in the northwestern part of the Indian subcontinent, where the Sindhu–Sarasvatī civilisation flourished, and both were familiar with copper.

questions.subject: Social Science
questions.topic: Understanding Early Indian State and Society
questions.stem:
A group of Class 9 students is making a short film on how India was governed in the earliest times, and they keep making the same mistake. One of them says that the earliest groups of people already had a fully formed State with laws and institutions to enforce them. Another says that nobody governed anybody at all. The teacher points out that what the two have to work out is not a single moment but a process: rules and shared norms that maintain order and harmony, and then, much later, organised political systems with rights and duties of rulers and subjects.

(a) State how rules and shared norms come into being, and what they do. (b) List the elements a State includes, and explain the condition in society under which such political systems developed. (c) Only two minutes of film are left; explain why discovering customs and practices alone would not be enough to show that a State existed.

answerScheme.modelAnswer: (a) Rules and shared norms evolve over time to maintain order and harmony, binding social groups into a unified whole. (b) A State is an organised political system based on rules and laws, with rights and duties of rulers and subjects and institutions for enforcing law and order. (c) Customs alone prove nothing, since society is primarily regulated by customs and practices rather than formal laws.

political system based on rules and laws. It includes well-defined
rights and duties of rulers and subjects, mechanisms of governance,
and institutions for enforcing law and order.

became larger and more complex.

(a) Kannauj, the main capital of the Gurjara–Pratihāras, in modern-day Uttar Pradesh.

Price (₹ per kg) | Quantity demanded of mangoes (kg) | Quantity supplied of mangoes (kg) | Outcome

markingPoints.description: At ₹40 per kg, demand of 38 kg exceeds supply of 6 kg, giving excess demand, a shortage (1)
At ₹150 per kg, supply of 43 kg exceeds demand of 8 kg, giving excess supply, a surplus (1)

Step 4: Equilibrium price = ₹100; equilibrium quantity = 12 kg.
Step 5: Prices stay stable here: there is no pressure to change, and neither a shortage nor a surplus.

हमारे देश की उच्चता और हीनता की कसौटी है है चुनाव। जिस देश के नागरिक यह समझते हैं कि चुनाव में किसे अपना मत देना चाहिए और किसे नहीं, वह देश उच्च है है। पर जहाँ के नागरिक गलत लोगों के उत्तेजक नारों या व्यक्‍त‍ियों के गलत प्रभाव में आकर मत देते हैं, वह हीन है है। इसलिए मतदान से पहले उम्मीदवार का चरित्र, उसकी योग्यता और उसके किए गए कामों को ध्यान से देखना चाहिए। किसी बड़े आदमी के कहने पर या किसी नारे के जोर पर अपना मत ऐसे व्यक्ति को दे देना, जो देश का निर्माण और सुधार नहीं कर सकता, देश के हित में नहीं है। हरेक नागरिक का यह कर्तव्य है कि वह जब भी कोई चुनाव हो, ठीक मनुष्य को अपना मत दें। यह उसका अधिकार भी है।

My First Attempt
Nobody in my family rides a bicycle, so when my father wheeled an old one out for me I was frightened of it. markingPoints.description: Content: consoles Anya and treats what she feels as a natural response to a loss rather than a mistake.

Expression: a warm, plain and supportive tone with correct spelling, punctuation and grammar.

answerScheme.modelAnswer:
Subject: Anya, please eat something today

Dear Anya,

Your grandmother died, and I am sorry. What you are feeling is not a mistake. Grief comes in many shapes — sadness, anger, guilt, loneliness, tiredness — and it is natural after any kind of loss, so do not tell yourself that you are doing it wrongly.

GRIEF AND FRIENDSHIP
A session for students who have lost someone

If you have lost a parent, a grandparent or a close friend, you are welcome here. Come and speak about it, or come and simply sit and listen; you decide which you can manage today. Grief is an emotion natural to all kinds of loss, and you will meet others whose sorrow has taken a different shape from yours. Accuracy: reflects that grief is an emotion natural to all kinds of loss and may appear as sadness, anger, guilt, loneliness or tiredness.
Expression: a clear and sympathetic style with correct spelling, punctuation and grammar.

answerScheme.modelAnswer:
WHAT A GRIEVING FRIEND NEEDS
When a classmate in school loses a parent, what helps is not advice but presence: sit beside them in the break, walk home with them, and go on talking about ordinary things until they can join in again. Grief is an emotion natural to all kinds of loss, and it wears many shapes — sadness, anger, guilt, loneliness, even tiredness — so never tell a grieving friend which feeling is the correct one. Be patient. Let them know that you care, and let them set the pace; some will want to talk about the loss, and some will not.

evidence: Although grief is unique and personal, a broad range of feelings and behaviours are commonly experienced after the death of a loved one.
Focusing on what we do for one another is the only consolation we can find.

markingPoints.description: Content: states that money was stolen from the clergyman's house, that the desk was opened and the housekeeping money was gone, and that nobody was seen
Format: begins with the heading NOTICE and gives the source (the village constable, Mr Jaffers) and the place, Iping, before the notice ends with the signature
Organisation: keeps the facts of the theft together first and sets the requests to residents as short separate numbered or bulleted points in a sensible order
Accuracy: uses correct grammar, spelling and punctuation, and keeps the formal impersonal tone a public notice requires
Expression: words the appeal briefly, clearly and politely, so that a reader knows at once what to do and whom to inform

answerScheme.modelAnswer:
NOTICE
From: The Village Constable, Mr Jaffers, Iping

Money has been stolen from the clergyman's house. The family was awakened by noises in the study, and found the desk opened and the housekeeping money gone. No one was seen. The village constable is investigating.

Villagers are requested to:
- Keep their doors locked and admit no stranger.
- Report any stranger seen about to the constable at once.
- Tell the constable at once if you notice anything strange in your house.
- Keep money in a safe place, not on a desk.

Your help will keep Iping safe.
Mr Jaffers, Village Constable

evidence: they heard the chink of money being taken from the clergyman’s desk.
Yet the desk had been opened and the housekeeping money was missing.
Mr Jaffers, the constable, now arrived

Subject: A Book You Will Not Put Down
Dear Friend,
I am writing to recommend The Invisible Man by H.G. Wells. It is the story of Griffin, a brilliant scientist who swallows certain rare drugs and makes his own body as transparent as a sheet of glass. He does not use the discovery well. He becomes a lawless wanderer who robs a shopkeeper and steals money from a desk, and nobody can see him. I chose it because it makes you think about whether science is used for good or for harm. You will enjoy it if you like adventure and mystery.
Yours sincerely,
Your Name

questions.subject: English
questions.stem: The Principal has asked you to speak at the school assembly on the value of science. Write a speech of about 100 words titled “Can a Man Become Invisible?”, and end with one line of advice for your listeners.

markingPoints.description: Content: names the scientist and how he made his body transparent, and says that he misused the discovery.
Format: opens with a greeting, keeps the spoken part short, and closes with “Thank you”.
Organisation: introduction, main point, a question put to the audience, one line of advice, and a closing.
Accuracy: correct tenses and punctuation, including the linked comparatives “as transparent as a sheet of glass” and “as solid as glass”.
Expression: spoken language addressed directly to the listeners, with at least one rhetorical question.

answerScheme.modelAnswer:
Good morning, everyone,
Have you ever wondered whether a man can become invisible? Griffin, a brilliant scientist, swallowed certain rare drugs and made his body as transparent as a sheet of glass and as solid as glass. He misused this discovery. He stole, and nobody could see him. Science gives us great power, but power must be used wisely. If you could be invisible today, would you use it to help others or to hide from them? I have one piece of advice. Use what you learn to serve others, never to deceive them.
Thank you.

make himself invisible. Does he use, or
misuse, his discovery?

person.

questions.subject: English
questions.stem: A scientist discovers that he can make his own body invisible, and the discovery leads him step by step to ruin. Trace that chain of events in order and give a reason for each step, beginning with the revenge he takes against his landlord and ending with the moment the constable Jaffers is knocked unconscious.

markingPoints.description: Griffin proved by experiment that the body could be made invisible, then swallowed rare drugs and became transparent like glass though still solid
When his landlord disliked him and tried to eject him, Griffin set fire to the house in revenge
To get away without being seen he had to remove his clothes, so with no clothes and no money he became a homeless wanderer, and he first became visible where he stepped in mud and left footprints
It was mid-winter and bitterly cold, so instead of walking the streets he slipped into a big London store and, after closing time, fitted himself out with warm clothes and slept on a pile of quilts
He overslept, panicked when the assistants arrived, ran from them and escaped only by taking off his newly-found clothes, leaving himself invisible and naked in the chill January air

At Drury Lane he bought a disguise and robbed the shopkeeper, then took a train to Iping, where, throwing off his bandages, whiskers, spectacles and nose, he fought unseen until Jaffers was knocked unconscious

answerScheme.modelAnswer:
1. Griffin proved by experiment that the human body could be made invisible, then swallowed rare drugs and turned transparent like a sheet of glass, though still as solid as glass.
2. His landlord disliked him and tried to eject him, so in revenge Griffin set fire to the house.
3. To get away without being seen he had to remove his clothes; with no clothes and no money he became a homeless wanderer, and he first showed where he had been when he stepped in mud and left footprints.
4. It was mid-winter and bitterly cold, so he slipped into a big London store and, after closing time, broke open boxes and fitted himself out with warm clothes, then slept on a pile of quilts.
5. He overslept, panicked when the assistants arrived, and escaped only by quickly taking off his newly-found clothes, leaving himself invisible and naked in the January chill.
6. At Drury Lane he bought a disguise, robbed the shopkeeper and took a train to Iping, where he threw off his false nose, whiskers and bandages and struck unseen blows until Jaffers was knocked unconscious.

evidence: His landlord disliked him and tried to eject him. In revenge Griffin set fire to the house.

To get away without being seen he had to remove his clothes. Thus it was that he became a homeless wanderer, without clothes, without money, and quite invisible — until he happened to step in some mud, and left footprints as he walked!
In the end Jaffers was knocked unconscious as he made a last attempt to hold on to the unseen scientist.

3. To escape unseen he removed his clothes and became a homeless wanderer. Reason: he had to leave the burning house.
4. He broke into a London store for warmth, then robbed a shopkeeper in Drury Lane. Reason: he had no money.
5. He took the housekeeping money from the clergyman's desk. Reason: he wanted more money.
6. Mrs Hall complained, so the constable Mr Jaffers was sent for and arrested him. Reason: his strange behaviour in the bedroom.

questions.subject: English
questions.stem: How did the people at Iping explain the strange things they saw in the scientist's rooms, and why were they so sure of their explanation?

markingPoints.description: The clergyman found the desk open and the money gone, though nobody was in the room.
Mrs Hall saw the hat leap up and the chair push her out and lock the door.
So she believed the room was haunted by spirits put there by the stranger.
The neighbours believed the trouble was witchcraft.
They were wrong because the man was no spirit; his body was simply transparent.
His sudden ready cash, after admitting he had none, made the suspicion stronger.

answerScheme.modelAnswer:
1. The clergyman and his wife heard the chink of money and found the desk open, but nobody was there. They looked under the desk, behind the curtains and even up the chimney.
2. Mrs Hall found the hat leaping into her face and the chair pushing her and her husband out and locking the door.
3. So Mrs Hall decided the room was haunted by spirits that the stranger had put into her furniture.
4. The neighbours decided the trouble was witchcraft.
5. Their explanation was wrong because the stranger was not a spirit at all; his body was transparent, so money and furniture could move while nobody saw him.
6. Suspicion grew when he suddenly produced ready cash after admitting that he had no money.

evidence:

and even up the chimney. There wasn’t a sign of anybody.

She was convinced

questions.subject: English
questions.stem: Griffin succeeded in making the human body transparent. Why did this discovery bring him misery instead of fame?

markingPoints.description: Griffin discovered how to make the human body transparent, but used it only for himself.

Because he could not be seen, he was never punished for it and went on misusing it.
He ended with no home, no money and no clothes, wandering in the bitter cold of mid-winter.
The villagers took him for an eccentric scientist and then suspected him of witchcraft.
He escaped again by throwing off one garment after another, so the discovery brought him only misery.

answerScheme.modelAnswer:
1. Griffin proved that the human body could become invisible, but he cared only for his own experiment.
2. He never used it to help anyone; he set fire to his landlord's house and robbed a shopkeeper in Drury Lane.
3. Because nobody could see him, he was never caught, and so he went on misusing it.
4. He had no friends and no money, and in mid-winter he could not do without clothes.
5. The villagers first took him for an eccentric scientist and then accused him of witchcraft.
6. He ended by throwing off one garment after another and escaping unseen, with no one able to lay hands on him.

evidence:
Griffin, the scientist, had carried out experiment after experiment
to prove that the human body could become invisible.
after which he robbed him of all the money he could find.

He had chosen
a bad time of the year to wander about London without clothes. It was
mid-winter.

SCIENCE EXHIBITION — SCHOOL NOTICE BOARD

Calling all students of Classes 9 and 10. The Annual Science Exhibition will be held in the school hall next month. Every entrant must display one project of his or her own work. Please put up a short note on the board used, the material needed and the time the work took. Entries will be closed on the last working day of this month. Projects that show real experiments and not only neat displays will be given priority. Enrol at the science laboratory during the lunch break. Come and make our exhibition worth visiting.

markingPoints.description: Content: the speech says clearly that the questions children ask are the beginning of scientific inquiry
Format: a salutation to the audience, the body of the speech and a concluding thank you
Organisation: a clear beginning, a middle part that gives everyday examples of wondering, and a short conclusion that sums up the message
Accuracy: correct spelling, punctuation, capital letters and a formal tone suitable for a school assembly
Expression: simple sentences and suitable vocabulary that hold the attention of the audience

answerScheme.modelAnswer:
Honourable Principal, teachers and dear friends,

I want to speak for a few minutes on a simple habit: asking questions. Children everywhere wonder about the world around them, and the questions they ask are the beginning of scientific inquiry. A boy who collects things and then asks what they are, or a child who asks why the rain falls in drops, has already taken the first step. So never be afraid to say, “I do not know, but I want to find out.” Curiosity is a cheap quality, and once you begin to ask questions, it stays with you.

Thank you.

evidence: Children everywhere wonder about the world around them.
The questions they ask are the beginning of scientific inquiry.
You also must have wondered about certain things around you.

After his freshman year at Harvard he identified the hormone's chemical structure, and the X-ray photos of that structure gave him the answer to how the cell can read the blueprint of its DNA.

questions.stem: Trace, step by step, how the loss of the borrowed necklace changed the life of the household, and say what their life was like before it was lost.

markingPoints.description: Before the loss they were poor but not in debt: he was a clerk at the Board of Education and she only suffered from the want of frocks and jewels.
She borrowed a diamond necklace from Mme Forestier and was the prettiest of all at the ball.
The necklace was lost in the cab; the dress, cloak and pockets were searched and the track on foot was walked over again.
M. Loisel went to the police and the cab offices and advertised a reward in the newspapers, but found nothing.
An identical necklace was bought for thirty-six thousand francs, the rest being borrowed from money-lenders.
They sent away the maid, took rooms in an attic, did the kitchen work themselves and lived like this for ten years, until the debt was cleared.

answerScheme.modelAnswer:
1. Before the loss they were poor but not in debt: M. Loisel was a clerk at the Board of Education, and his wife suffered only from the want of frocks and jewels.
2. She borrowed a diamond necklace from Mme Forestier and was the prettiest of all at the ball.
3. In the cab home the necklace was lost; the dress, cloak and pockets were searched.
4. M. Loisel walked back over the track they had gone on foot, went to the police and the cab offices, and advertised a reward.
5. Nothing was found, so they bought an identical necklace for thirty-six thousand francs, borrowing the rest from money-lenders.
6. They sent away the maid, took rooms in an attic and did the kitchen work themselves for ten years, until the debt was cleared.

questions.subject: English
questions.stem: In the last few lines a friend tells the heroine that the necklace she lent was false. Why does this come as a shock to the reader, and what does it suggest about the ten years the family spent paying for it?

markingPoints.description: The replacement necklace was valued at forty thousand francs and bought for thirty-six thousand.
The family paid by sending away the maid, moving to an attic, doing the kitchen work, and the husband copying at five sous a page.
The friend then admits that her own necklace was false and not worth over five hundred francs.
A fortune was therefore spent on an imitation of a worthless jewel, which is the source of the reader's shock.
It shows how one evening's desire to appear rich can be carried to ruin.
It throws doubt on the wife's claim that all her misery was caused by her friend, for the fault lay in her own pride.

answerScheme.modelAnswer:
1. The reader has already been shown the price: the replacement necklace was valued at forty thousand francs and bought for thirty-six thousand.
2. To pay it the family gave up its maid, moved into an attic, did the kitchen work, and had the husband copy pages at five sous by night.
3. Then the friend admits that her own necklace was false and not worth over five hundred francs.
4. So the whole sacrifice rests on costume jewellery, and the sum paid was many times its real value.
5. The shock shows how far one evening's wish to appear rich can be carried.
6. It also casts doubt on the wife's claim that all her misery was caused by her friend, for the fault lay in her own pride.

evidence: It was valued at forty thousand francs. They could get it for thirty-six thousand.
Mine were false. They were not worth over five hundred francs!

2. Reason: The cranial nerves that arise from the brain are the nerves that carry messages between the central nervous system and the other parts of the body.

The
brain and spinal cord constitute the central nervous system (Fig. 6.3).

by the peripheral nervous system consisting of cranial nerves arising

questions.stem:
Assertion: When gametes from two different plants fuse during sexual reproduction, the new plant that forms carries the number of chromosomes and the DNA content of a single plant rather than twice that amount, because the cells that give rise to the gametes hold only half the number of chromosomes and half the amount of DNA found in the non-reproductive body cells.
2. Reason: This halving of the chromosomes and the DNA in those cells is brought about by a process of cell division called meiosis.
Choose the correct option: (A) Both 1 and 2 are true and 2 is the correct explanation for 1 (B) Both 1 and 2 are true but 2 is not the correct explanation for 1 (C) 1 is true but 2 is false (D) Both 1 and 2 are false

answerScheme.modelAnswer: Both 1 and 2 are true and 2 is the correct explanation for 1

evidence:
One solution that many multi-cellular
organisms have found for the problem mentioned above is to have special
lineages of cells in specialised organs in which only half the number of
chromosomes and half the amount of DNA as compared to the non-
reproductive body cells.

This is achieved by a process of cell division
called meiosis. Thus, when these germ-cells from two individuals combine
during sexual reproduction to form a new individual, it results in re-
establishment of the number of chromosomes and the DNA content in
the new generation.

After fertilisation, the zygote divides several times to form an
embryo within the ovule. The ovule develops a tough coat and is
gradually converted into a seed. The ovary grows rapidly and ripens

questions.stem:
A biology teacher explains to her class why a child does not end up with twice as much DNA as either parent. She says that sexual reproduction combines the DNA of two different individuals, and that if this happened generation after generation, each new generation would carry twice the DNA of the one before and the control of the cellular apparatus by the DNA would be upset. She adds that many multi-cellular organisms get around this by keeping special lineages of cells in specialised organs, and by a cell division that halves both the chromosome number and the DNA. The students ask her to name that division and to say what happens when two such cells unite.

Name the cell division that halves the number of chromosomes and the amount of DNA, and say in what kind of cells this halving is found. (ii) The teacher says each new generation would otherwise carry twice the DNA of the previous one. State what would happen to the control of the cellular apparatus by the DNA. (iii) When two such cells from different individuals unite during sexual reproduction, explain why the number of chromosomes and the DNA content of the new generation stays the same as before.

answerScheme.modelAnswer: (i) Meiosis, found in special lineages of cells in specialised organs. (ii) The control of the cellular apparatus by the DNA would be messed up. (iii) Each cell already carries half, so their fusion re-establishes the number of chromosomes and the DNA content in the new generation.

evidence:
One solution that many multi-cellular
organisms have found for the problem mentioned above is to have special
lineages of cells in specialised organs in which only half the number of
chromosomes and half the amount of DNA as compared to the non-
reproductive body cells. This is achieved by a process of cell division
called meiosis.

questions.stem:
A gardener plants mustard and papaya in the same garden and watches the flowers open. In the mustard flower she finds both stamens and a pistil, while the papaya flower seems to carry only one of the two. She also notices a faint yellowish powder on her fingers after she touches a stamen, and she wants to know which part of the flower it came from and how it reaches the ovules. A student in the class explains that the pollen must first land on a stigma, and that a tube then carries it down through the style to the ovary, where the female germ-cells lie.

Name the type of flower found in the mustard plant and in the papaya plant, and say which reproductive parts each of them contains. (ii) Name the three parts of the pistil in order from the swollen base upwards, and say which of them contains the ovules. (iii) Once the pollen has landed on a suitable stigma, explain how the male germ-cell reaches the ovule, and state what its fusion with the female gamete there produces.

answerScheme.modelAnswer: (i) Mustard is bisexual, with both stamens and pistil; papaya is unisexual, with either stamens or pistil. (ii) Ovary, style and stigma; the ovary holds the ovules. (iii) A tube grows out of the pollen grain and travels through the style to the ovary, where the male germ-cell fuses with the female gamete to form a zygote.

evidence:
The flower may be unisexual (papaya,
watermelon) when it contains either stamens
or pistil or bisexual (Hibiscus, mustard)
when it contains both stamens and pistil.

The swollen bottom part is the ovary, middle elongated part is the style
and the terminal part which may be sticky is the stigma. The ovary
contains ovules and each ovule has an egg cell. The male germ-cell
produced by pollen grain fuses with the female gamete present in
the ovule.

After the pollen lands on a suitable stigma, it has to reach the
female germ-cells which are in the ovary. For this, a tube grows
out of the pollen grain and travels through the style to reach the
ovary.

questions.stem:
After pollen has been carried to the stigma of a flower, a grower tags it and returns a week later. The petals, sepals, stamens, style and stigma have all shrivelled and dropped off, but the base of the flower has swollen into something the family can eat, and inside it there are hard little structures each holding a miniature plant. The grower has read that the two germ-cells that met inside the flower came from the parents, one large enough to carry its own food and the other small and motile. She wants to know how those two cells produced what she is now holding.

Name the part of the flower that becomes the edible swelling, and name the hard structures found inside it. (ii) Starting from the fusion of the male germ-cell with the female gamete in the ovule, name the structure formed first and trace the changes that produce the seed and the fruit. (iii) Both germ-cells differ from one another, and the larger one carries stores the other does not. Name both germ-cells and say how these stores help the zygote to develop.

answerScheme.modelAnswer: (i) The ovary becomes the fruit; the hard structures inside are seeds. (ii) Fertilisation gives a zygote, which divides to form an embryo in the ovule; the ovule turns into the seed. (iii) The larger germ-cell is the female gamete, whose food-stores give the zygote the energy to develop into an organism with specialised tissues and organs.

evidence:
After fertilisation, the zygote divides several times to form an
embryo within the ovule. The ovule develops a tough coat and is
gradually converted into a seed. The ovary grows rapidly and ripens
to form a fruit.

One germ-cell is large and contains the food-stores while the
other is smaller and likely to be motile. Conventionally, the motile germ-
cell is called the male gamete and the germ-cell containing the stored
food is called the female gamete.

If the zygote is to grow and develop into an organism which has
highly specialised tissues and organs, then it has to have sufficient stores
of energy for doing this.

questions.subject: Science
questions.topic: Do Organisms Create Exact Copies of Themselves?
questions.stem:
A student asks her teacher whether a baby is an exact copy of its parents. The teacher says DNA copying is accurate, and that if it were less accurate many of the copies made would not be able to work with the cellular apparatus and would die. A new variation, she adds, is made in a DNA copy that already carries variations gathered over earlier generations, so two individuals in a population have quite different patterns of accumulated variation, and since these variations sit in living individuals they do no real harm. Combining variations from two individuals therefore gives a novel combination, she says, and that is exactly what sexual reproduction does.

State what would happen to many of the DNA copies produced if the copying mechanism were less accurate, and say where a new variation is made. (ii) Explain why the variations carried by different individuals in a population can be combined safely, and why each new combination of variants is novel.

answerScheme.modelAnswer: (i) The copies would not work with the cellular apparatus and would die; a new variation arises in a DNA copy that already carries variations from earlier generations. (ii) All the variations sit in living individuals and so do no real harm; combining the variations of two different individuals creates a novel combination of variants.

evidence:
If the DNA copying mechanisms were to be less accurate, many
of the resultant DNA copies would not be able to work with the cellular
apparatus, and would die.

Each new variation is made in a DNA copy that already
has variations accumulated from previous generations.

Since all of these variations are in living
individuals, it is assured that they do not have any really bad effects.
Combining variations from two or more individuals would thus create
new combinations of variants. Each combination would be novel, since
it would involve two different individuals.

Riya is reading a printed page in the evening. Read the case below and answer the three questions that follow.

When she holds it very close to her eyes the letters look blurred and her eyes begin to strain, so she moves the page away until she can read it comfortably. (i) State what happens to the curvature, the thickness and the focal length of the eye lens when Riya looks at the nearby page.
(ii) State the minimum distance at which a young adult with normal vision sees an object most distinctly without strain, and give the name for this distance.

answerScheme.modelAnswer: (i) The ciliary muscles contract, so the lens becomes more curved and thicker and its focal length decreases. Ravi is sitting beside a long straight copper wire through which current is flowing. He grips the wire in his right hand with his thumb pointing in the direction of the current and finds that his fingers wrap round the wire in a definite direction. On the terrace above him, a power line runs across the sky. Read the case below and answer the three questions that follow.
Ravi is sitting beside a long straight copper wire through which current is flowing. He grips the wire in his right hand with his thumb pointing in the direction of the current and finds that his fingers wrap round the wire in a definite direction. On the terrace above him, a power line runs across the sky. His father, an electrician, tells him that the current in that line flows from east to west, and asks him what a compass needle placed at a point directly below the line would do, and what one placed directly above the line would do. Ravi wonders whether he can work out both answers without going up to the line.
(i) State the rule that fixes the direction in which Ravi's fingers wrap round the wire, and name the part of the hand that must point along the current.
(ii) State the direction in which the magnetic field turns at a point directly below the power line when it is viewed from the east end, and when it is viewed from the west end.
(iii) Ravi says the field below the line and the field above the line must turn in opposite senses. Analysing what the rule says about a plane perpendicular to the wire, comment on his claim and state the direction of the magnetic field at a point below and at a point above the line.

answerScheme.modelAnswer: (i) The right-hand thumb rule; the thumb points along the current. (ii) Clockwise from the east end, anti-clockwise from the west end, in a plane perpendicular to the wire. (iii) The rule works for any current-carrying straight conductor, and at both points the field turns clockwise seen from the east end and anti-clockwise seen from the west end, so Ravi need not climb up.

conductor in the direction of the field lines of the magnetic field, as

thumb rule, we get that the magnetic field (at any point below or
above the wire) turns clockwise in a plane perpendicular to the wire,
when viewed from the east end, and anti-clockwise, when viewed

Meera's teacher bends a long straight copper wire into a circular loop and passes a current through it. She asks the class to imagine the pattern of magnetic field lines all around the loop, and reminds them of what they had seen for a straight wire. Two students disagree: one says the coil is stronger only because the wire is longer, the other says it is stronger because the turns act one upon another.

Read the case below and answer the three questions that follow.
Meera's teacher bends a long straight copper wire into a circular loop and passes a current through it. She asks the class to imagine the pattern of magnetic field lines all around the loop, and reminds them of what they had seen for a straight wire. She then holds up a circular coil wound with many turns and asks how the field of this coil compares with the field of a single turn carrying the same current. Two students disagree: one says the coil is stronger only because the wire is longer, the other says it is stronger because the turns act one upon another.
(i) State how the pattern of magnetic field lines around a current-carrying circular loop compares with the pattern around a current-carrying straight wire.
(ii) State the shape in which the field lines appear at the centre of the circular loop, and give the reason.
(iii) Meera's coil has n turns and carries the same current as a single turn. Analysing why the field due to each turn adds up, state how much larger the field of the coil is than that of the single turn, and comment on the claim that the coil is stronger only because the wire is longer.

answerScheme.modelAnswer: (i) Concentric circles growing larger away from the wire, as for a straight wire. (ii) Straight lines at the centre, where the arcs of the big circles appear straight. (iii) The field is n times that of a single turn, since each turn carries current in the same direction and the fields add up; the extra strength comes from the turns, not the wire length.

evidence:
Similarly at every point of a current-carrying
circular loop, the concentric circles representing the magnetic
field around it would become larger and larger as we move
away from the wire (Fig. 12.8).

By the time we reach at the
centre of the circular loop, the arcs of these big circles would
appear as straight lines.

Therefore, if there is a circular coil having n turns, the field produced is
n times as large as that produced by a single turn. This is because the

questions.topic: What Development Promises — Different People, Different Goals
questions.stem: Two countries report exactly the same average income. In one, people are neither very rich nor extremely poor; in the other, most citizens are poor and one person is extremely rich. A reporter concludes that the two countries are equally developed. Explain why average income alone does not support her conclusion.

markingPoints.description: Average income does not tell us how the income is distributed among people
In the first country people are neither very rich nor extremely poor
In the other country most citizens are poor while one person is extremely rich, so equal averages do not mean equal development

answerScheme.modelAnswer: Average income is useful for comparison but it does not tell us how that income is distributed among people. In the first country people are neither very rich nor extremely poor, so income is widely shared. In the other, most citizens are poor and one person is extremely rich. The same average therefore hides very different distributions, so equal averages do not mean equal development.

questions.stem:
A school social science club decided to find out how developed three states are. They collected the per capita income of Haryana, Kerala and Bihar for 2023–24: Rs 3,25,759, Rs 2,81,001 and Rs 60,337. They also noted the infant mortality rate per 1,000 live births — Haryana 28, Kerala 6, Bihar 27 — and the literacy rate: Haryana 82 per cent, Kerala 94 per cent and Bihar 62 per cent. When they wrote up their findings, one group said Haryana was the most developed because its per capita income was the highest. Another group said Kerala was ahead, because it came first on two of the three measures. The club asked its teacher to settle the argument.

On per capita income alone, name the state that ranks first and the state that ranks last. (ii) On infant mortality rate per 1,000 live births, name the state with the lowest figure and the state with the highest figure. (iii) On all three measures together, which state comes out ahead, and why can per capita income alone not settle the argument?

answerScheme.modelAnswer: (i) Haryana first, Bihar last. (ii) Kerala lowest at 6, Haryana highest at 28. (iii) Kerala comes out ahead, leading on two of the three measures; per capita income is only one attribute and says nothing about how income is distributed among people.

questions.stem:
Two students argued about what counts as progress. One said a place is developed when its people earn more on average. The other said that people think of better income but also keep in mind security, respect for others, equal treatment and freedom, and that when we think of a nation or a region we may, besides average income, think of other equally important attributes. A class survey asked everyone to name one thing that would make their own area better. Few students named money; most named security, equal treatment, respect for others or freedom. The teacher asked the two students to settle their argument with these answers.

Which goals do people keep in mind besides better income? (ii) Apart from average income, what kind of attributes may we think about when we judge a nation or a region? (iii) Why does the class survey support the second student's claim, and how would you answer the first student?

answerScheme.modelAnswer: (i) Security, respect for others, equal treatment and freedom. (ii) Other equally important attributes, such as those goals. (iii) Few students named money and most named security, equal treatment, respect or freedom, so income is only one attribute and cannot by itself show how far a nation has developed.

The capital city Brussels breaks this pattern: 80 per cent of its people speak French while 20 per cent are Dutch-speaking. So the Dutch-speaking people are a majority in the country as a whole, but a minority in the capital.

questions.subject: Social Science
questions.stem:
Sri Lanka is an island nation just a few kilometres off the southern coast of Tamil Nadu, with about two crore people, about the same as in Haryana. Like other nations in the South Asia region, it has a diverse population. The major social groups are the Sinhala-speakers, at 74 per cent, and the Tamil-speakers, at 18 per cent. Among the Tamils there are two sub-groups: Tamil natives of the country are called Sri Lankan Tamils (13 per cent), and the rest, whose forefathers came from India as plantation workers during the colonial period, are called Indian Tamils. Sri Lankan Tamils are concentrated in the north and east of the country.

(a) What share of Sri Lanka's population speaks Tamil, and into how many sub-groups are Tamil-speakers divided? (b) Name the sub-group whose forefathers came from India as plantation workers during the colonial period. (c) Explain why the Tamil-speakers of Sri Lanka do not behave as one single compact group.

answerScheme.modelAnswer: (a) Tamil-speakers are 18 per cent and are divided into two sub-groups. (b) Indian Tamils. (c) One sub-group consists of natives of the country, concentrated in the north and east, while the other descends from forefathers who came from India as plantation workers during the colonial period, so they have different origins and locations.

questions.subject: Social Science
questions.stem:
The minority French-speaking community in Belgium was relatively rich and powerful. This was resented by the Dutch-speaking community, who got the benefit of economic development and education much later. This resentment led to tensions between the Dutch-speaking and French-speaking communities during the 1950s and 1960s. The tension between the two communities was more acute in Brussels, because there the Dutch speakers were a minority. If the Dutch community took advantage of its numeric majority and forced its will on the French and German-speaking populations, the conflict would be pushed further.

(a) Which community in Belgium was relatively rich and powerful, and which community resented it? (b) During which period did the tensions between the two communities appear? (c) Explain why a political settlement in which one community simply forces its will on the others is dangerous for Belgium.

answerScheme.modelAnswer: (a) The French-speaking minority was relatively rich and powerful, and the Dutch-speaking community resented it. (b) During the 1950s and 1960s. (c) The Dutch community's numeric majority could be used to force its will on the French and German speakers, which would push the conflict among the communities further.

questions.stem: Priya reads that in the city of Porto Alegre in Brazil, local inhabitants take real decisions about their own city through meetings held in every sector, and that about 20,000 people join in this decision making every year. In about 75 words, and in steps, explain how the city combines decentralisation with participative democracy, and state the changes this method has brought about.

markingPoints.description: A parallel organisation operates alongside the municipal council, enabling local inhabitants to take real decisions for their city
The city is divided into sectors or wards, and each sector has a meeting, like that of the gram sabha, in which anyone living in that area can participate
Any citizen can participate in the meetings that discuss issues affecting the entire city, and the budget of the city is discussed in these meetings
About 20,000 people participate in this decision making exercise every year
Money can no longer be spent only for the benefit of the colonies where rich people live; buses run to the poor colonies and builders cannot evict slum-dwellers without resettling them

answerScheme.modelAnswer: Step 1: A parallel organisation works alongside the municipal council, so that local inhabitants take real decisions for their city. Step 2: The city is divided into sectors or wards, and each sector has a meeting, like that of the gram sabha, in which anyone living in that area can participate. Step 3: Any citizen can also join the meetings that discuss issues affecting the entire city, where the budget of the city is discussed. Step 4: About 20,000 people take part in this decision making exercise every year. Step 5: Money can no longer be spent only for the colonies where rich people live; buses run to the poor colonies and builders cannot evict slum-dwellers without resettling them.

questions.stem:
Rohan's town holds regular elections and has an elected council. Rohan is sure that because the council is chosen by the people, it will fix every local problem on its own: the leaking taps, the unlit streets and the school roof. He tells his friend Meera that she should stop complaining and simply wait for democracy to deliver. Meera agrees that democracy deserves support, and yet she points out that her neighbours are not at all satisfied with democracy in practice, even though they prefer it to rule by a monarch or to military or religious leaders. She says a democracy can only create conditions, and asks Rohan who must then do the rest.

Read the case below and answer the questions that follow. (a) Rohan believes the elected council will fix every local problem on its own. State what a democracy can do by itself, and who has to do the rest. (b) Meera says her neighbours prefer democracy to rule by a monarch or to military or religious leaders, and yet are not satisfied with it. Name the situation she is describing. (c) Rohan says that if the taps are still leaking after the election, democracy has failed. Using what Meera says, explain why this verdict is not justified and what Rohan should do instead.

answerScheme.modelAnswer: (a) It can only create conditions for achieving something; the citizens have to take advantage of them. (b) A dilemma: democracy is good in principle but not so good in practice. (c) A democracy creates conditions only, so unrepaired taps are not proof that democracy has failed; citizens must use those conditions to reach their goals.

markingPoints.description: विषय-वस्तु: बच्चे की दंतुरित मुसकान का प्रभाव — मृतक में भी जान डाल देती है और कठोर से कठोर मन पिघला देती है।

प्रारूप: शीर्षक सहित एक ही सतत अनुच्छेद के रूप में लगभग १२० शब्दों की रचना।

questions.subject: Hindi
questions.stem: आपके विद्यालय की पत्रिका के लिए 'संगीत-साधना और लगन' विषय पर लगभग १२० शब्दों का एक सुसंगत अनुच्छेद लिखिए।

markingPoints.description: विषय-वस्तु: संगीत को आराधना माना तथा उसके विधि-विधान, शास्त्र और गुरु-शिष्य परंपरा का उल्लेख।
विषय-वस्तु: बिस्मिल्ला खाँ द्वारा अस्सी बरस तक निभाई गई साधना और उनमें लगन व धैर्य।
विषय-वस्तु: अभ्यास, पूर्ण तन्मयता, धैर्य और मंथन की आवश्यकता का कथन तथा आज के संदर्भ में उसका महत्त्व।
प्रारूप: शीर्षक सहित एक ही सतत अनुच्छेद के रूप में लगभग १२० शब्दों की रचना।
व्यवस्था: परिचय, उदाहरण और निष्कर्ष के क्रम में तर्कसंगठित प्रवाह।
भाषा-शुद्धता एवं प्रसाद: सही वर्तनी, व्याकरण, विराम-चिह्न तथा सरल प्रभावशाली भाषा का प्रयोग।

answerScheme.modelAnswer: संगीत कोई मनोरंजन का साधन नहीं, एक आराधना है। इसका विधि-विधान है, शास्त्र है और गुरु-शिष्य परंपरा भी। शहनाई के महान वादक उस्ताद बिस्मिल्ला खाँ ने अस्सी बरस तक यही साधना निभाई। उनमें लगन और धैर्य ऐसा था कि वृद्धावस्था में भी उनकी साधना चलती रही। उन्होंने बताया कि संगीत केवल परिचय से नहीं, उसके अभ्यास से सीखा जाता है और उसके लिए पूर्ण तन्मयता, धैर्य तथा मंथन ज़रूरी है। आज जब हमारे विद्यालयों में संगीत सिखाया जाता है, तब ये बातें हमें याद दिलाती हैं कि संगीत में सफलता बिना लगन और अभ्यास के संभव नहीं। यही लगन हमारी पीढ़ी को भी सफल बनाने वाली है।

evidence:
उन्होंने यह भी स्पष्ट किया है कि संगीत
एक आराधना है। इसका विधि-विधान है। इसका शास्त्र है, इस शास्त्र से परिचय
आवश्यक है, सिर्फ़ परिचय ही नहीं उसका अभ्यास ज़रूरी है और अभ्यास के लिए
गुरु-शिष्य परंपरा ज़रूरी है, पूर्ण तन्मयता ज़रूरी है, धैर्य ज़रूरी है, मंथन ज़रूरी है।

वह लगन और धैर्य बिस्मिल्ला खाँ में रहा है। तभी 80 वर्ष की उम्र में भी उनकी
साधना चलती रही है।

संगीत नाटक अकादमी पुरस्कार एवं पद्मविभूषण जैसे सम्मानों से नहीं, बल्कि अपनी अजेय
संगीतयात्रा के लिए बिस्मिल्ला खाँ साहब भविष्य में हमेशा संगीत के नायक बने रहेंगे। नब्बे
वर्ष की भरी-पूरी आयु में 21 अगस्त 2006 को संगीत रसिकों की हार्दिक सभा से विदा
हुए खाँ साहब की सबसे बड़ी देन हमें यही है कि पूरे अस्सी बरस उन्होंने संगीत को संपूर्णता
व एकाधिकार से सीखने की जिजीविषा को अपने भीतर जिंदा रखा।
